prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms held at the magic wavelength opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I change my configuration: I drop IceCube and propose optical lattice clocks (Katori, Ye) as the whole prize. My round-1 pairing rested on the idea that a new instrument made the discovery possible, and that holds for the lattice clock. Katori's magic-wavelength condition cancels the trapping light shift, so thousands of atoms are interrogated at once, and the many-atom regime has been brought to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. As an experimentalist, what I look for is independent confirmation, and this has it: clocks in Japan, the US, Europe and China are compared against each other and agree at that level, and they already resolve gravitational redshift across millimetres and constrain the constancy of constants. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, two names, Katori for the proposal and first strontium realisation and Ye for the accuracy frontier and many-body regime. In answer to the chair's own question on distinctness: the comb (2005) gave a way to count optical cycles and the ion work (2012) gave control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock showed that a large ensemble can be held in a light trap with the trap's perturbation engineered away, so that stability and accuracy are both reached at once. That is a new physical condition, not only a better instrument.
statement.case_against: Distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a real judgment call, and Jun Ye's comb work already sits in an earlier prize context. Lemonde, Ludlow, Lemke, Takamoto, Derevianko and Bloom are left out by a two-name credit, and the record accuracy is shared between laboratories and will be superseded. The redefinition of the second is still pending. Above all, B024 is the most broadly supported candidate in the committee (seven of eight ranked it) and I rank it only fourth because it lies outside my expertise; if the condensed-matter members converge on one defensible trio, I would not stand in its way, and B024 is my first alternative. A single-topic B001 prize is also less broad than a two-part prize, but I will not build a compromise out of two unrelated topics when one half, IceCube with a single name, cannot be defended.

responses.point: Moves B024 to first place, keeps IceCube as an alternative, and says a one-person prize for a collaboration of hundreds invites a credit dispute that this list cannot settle.
responses.response: You are right and I am persuaded. We were the only two who put IceCube first, and when I asked what the alternative to one name was, neither of us could give a three-name answer that is faithful to AMANDA, DUMAND and the later directors. I withdraw B021 from my preferred configuration and keep it as an alternative for a year when the credit can be settled. On B024 you asked me to judge by confirmation, and I do: it is exceptional, and I place it as my first alternative. What I still cannot judge is the choice between your trio and Johansson's.

responses.point: Ranks the lattice clock first as a new way of measuring, with independent reproduction at 1e-18, and asks whether the pending redefinition of the second troubles me.
responses.response: No. I treat the redefinition as depending on the achievement and not as a precondition for it. The performance is already demonstrated by several laboratories comparing clocks independently, which is what I would want to see before a prize, and waiting for the redefinition would make the prize follow a metrology decision rather than a discovery. I accept your point that your Boulder year means you are close to the field, and I read your support with that in mind, but my own support does not depend on yours.

responses.point: Pushes back on calling the lattice clock instrument development, arguing that the magic-wavelength condition is a physics insight and the many-atom regime brings collective effects, and notes the single-name IceCube problem.
responses.response: I accept the push-back and I have changed my wording. The magic-wavelength condition is a statement about light shifts that makes the scheme possible, and a many-atom clock at ion-level uncertainty is not just a better version of an earlier device. I therefore put the citation on the magic-wavelength lattice itself, and not on records or on practical uses. I also agree your remark about IceCube was fair, which is why I have dropped it. Your disclosed closeness to atomic structure does not change my reading of the confirmation record.

responses.point: Now prefers topological insulators with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, arguing the 3D observation would otherwise go unrecognised, and says the case weakens if no defensible trio exists.
responses.response: I take the 3D point seriously, and it is the main reason I would not obstruct B024. But your trio and Mehlig's and Danielsson's trio disagree on whether Hasan or Mele is the third name, and I am not able to settle that as an astroparticle physicist. That unsettled allocation is why I do not yet move B024 to the main position; if the committee agrees on one trio in this round, I would vote for it with a clear conscience. I also note your disclosed connection to circuit QED and agree you were right to keep B029 only as an alternative.

responses.point: Argues that topological insulators are a general organising principle with a bulk invariant, that Kane and Mele should not be split, and that Molenkamp is the experimental anchor.
responses.response: Your argument that the Z2 theory should not split Kane and Mele is persuasive, and it makes the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio look better to me than the one I proposed. Against that, you yourself write that omitting Hasan, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, is a real cost. I read that as a case where the science is sound but the credit will be argued about in public for years. For that reason I prefer the clock, where I can describe the credited contributions in a sentence each, but I would treat a unified condensed-matter recommendation as a legitimate alternative outcome.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes or as one precision-metrology lineage.
Whether the condensed-matter members will converge on one defensible B024 trio, which would make it a stronger main prize than B001 given its broader support.
I am outside atomic physics and condensed matter, and rely on colleagues for the credit questions in B001 and B024.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes recognition now premature, though I read it as dependent on the achievement and not a precondition.
statement.conflict_note: Updated: my round-1 field familiarity with IceCube no longer applies to my configuration since I have dropped B021. I have no collaboration, institutional or personal link to Katori or Ye; my work in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur is in astroparticle physics and detector development, not atomic or precision-measurement physics. As chair I note Kroll's and Lindroth's disclosed field proximity to B001 and weigh their views accordingly.
